chunks: And from him (Al-Hilli) from Al-Qasim ibn Muhammad from Al-Husayn ibn Abi al-'Ala' who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'A man rises [for prayer] and it has already become light in the morning.' He said: 'Let him pray the two prostrations (rak'ahs) that are before the morning prayer, then let him pray the morning prayer.'

Thus, these two narrations clarify that what is meant by those hadiths is the first dawn (Al-Fajr al-Awwal). This is because the first hadith mentions the time between you and the light being level with your head, which is an indication of the first dawn that rises vertically. Similarly, the other hadith mentions 'the man rises and it has become light in the morning,' which indicates a slight light. The second dawn (Al-Fajr al-Thani) is not like that; rather, its light is widespread and abundant in the sky's horizon.

It is also possible that these narrations came as a form of precautionary dissimulation (Taqiyyah), while conceding that the dawn referred to in them is the second dawn, because among our opponents, it is held that these two rak'ahs are not prayed except after the rising of the second dawn.
And that which reveals what we have mentioned is what he narrated:

key_terms.السَّجْدَتَيْنِ: The two prostrations (referring to the two rak'ahs of sunnah prayer)

ai.seo_question: When should the two sunnah rak'ahs of the morning prayer be performed relative to the two dawns?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi utilizes this narration from Al-Husayn ibn Abi al-‘Ala’ to resolve the juristic debate regarding whether the two sunnah rak'ahs of Fajr must be prayed before or after the onset of the second dawn (sunrise). By distinguishing between the slender vertical light of the first dawn and the widespread horizontal light of the second, the text establishes that the preferred time for these voluntary prayers is during the first dawn, while acknowledging that Taqiyyah may explain variations in other reports. This analysis underscores the Shia emphasis on precise temporal markers in ritual practice, linking astronomical phenomena directly to legal rulings.
